body: Zalloua, Z. (2024). Zahi Zalloua is Cushing Eells Professor of Philosophy and Literature and Director of IRES at Whitman College. He is also Editor of The Comparatist. His recent teaching and scholarship engage Critical Black Studies, the Posthuman, and the Palestinian Question. The politics of the wretched: Race, reason, and Ressentiment. Bloomsbury Academic, Bloomsbury Publishing Plc. // newsci dele-phant
Bad affects invade the lives of the wretched; they seep into your unconscious and condition your waking life. Your ressentiment
—this book’s bad affect of choice—
is often judged from without.
The Left and the Right caution against its
corrosive
presence
and negative impact on your perception of the world. Though motivated by drastically different reasons (

the former worries that an attachment to woundedness commits you to an identitarian logic with a limited emancipatory vision while the latter decries the culture of grievances fueled by minority identity politics

), there is a shared suspicion that ressentiment will damage a sense of the common good—either by undermining the political aspirations of the wretched, corrupting what is good for the individuals of the Global South, or by threatening the ruling class, striking irrationally, violently, and angerly at their possession of and claim over the good. I have sought to paint a different picture of ressentiment, which, as I see it, is still too often tainted by Nietzsche’s powerful indictment.

Ressentiment is to be neither overcome nor fetishized. It is to be lived with. Because it arises within a relation to self and to others, ressentiment involves an ethics and a politics—a care for the self and a care
(or the lack thereof)
for others

—with all the ambiguities that the concepts of self and other (fellow wretched, ally, friend, foe, etc.) necessarily entail. And since ressentiment’s future lies in the force of its undoings and/as inventions, in what it introduces into social existence (to recall Fanon’s formulation), an aesthetic register equally mediates the affect’s articulation and deployment. Ressentiment creates; what it brings into the world, and for what purpose, should concern us all.
To live with ressentiment is to navigate a condition imposed on you like an illness but also to tap its resourceful energy, the dynamism co-constituted by self and ressentiment.

To hazard the analogy of illness is to risk pathologizing ressentiment, pulling us back into the Nietzschean orbit that I have argued we need to exit, pulling us away from the libidinal and material conditions of the socio-economic world. And yet the question of illness is not completely misleading or irrelevant to our discussion. Quite the contrary, the ressentimental reason of the wretched repeatedly asks, what does normalcy (the absence of mental disorders) mean for Blacks in an anti-Black world, for Palestinians in a settler-colonial state, for Beurs in a neocolonial regime, for the precariously employed and unemployed in a neoliberal capitalist system? If there is
pathology
, its
origins
are
found in the structures of the world, a world that many inhabit painfully, a world that punishes the wretched, exploits them, and/or racializes them

. Ressentiment, then, does begin in a wounded self, but this affect can, and must, undergo a dislocation. If it doesn’t, ressentiment’s inertia might push it into the hands of the new priests of identity politics, today’s managers and manipulators of bad affects— traickers in their private use. But this is not ressentiment’s destiny. In its public use,
ressentiment explodes all kinds of futurologies; it confounds any imputed teleology
. Its ontology is profoundly relational—alterity is a fundamental feature of ressentiment’s being and doing.

Attesting to and sustaining a collective utopian demand for more, the No! of the wretched is enacted in the name of robbed realities and destroyed worlds. It proceeds by breaking the bewitching powers of liberal, and neoliberal, ideology, which reside in its ability to normalize desire and paper over the existence of social antagonisms.

This ideology’s manicured presentation of social reality tells us capitalism is the only game in town—banishing class struggle from the lexicon, the cultural imaginary—and assures us that “progress” and “democracy” are vibrant features of our world. Its predominant face is fetishist disavowal. Yes, I know very well that American society is experiencing racial lareups, but, all the same, let’s not forget that
the arc of history bends toward justice.

Ressentiment is born of this fundamental gap between what the world is and what its backers purport it to be: colorblind and equally shared by all of us. Ressentiment’s raison d’ être, the aim of its labor, lies in its indefatigable will to disturb this alluring but deceptive and cruel picture of the world. Ressentiment indexes an unconscionable reality, a problem, a pain—the fact of being cheated.1 True, ressentimental subjects are prone to strike at the wrong target, often those in a weaker position. This is why ressentiment needs reason. But reason cannot assume the position of dominance and proceed to disabuse/cure the subject of her ressentiment; reason must learn to recognize that there is a rationality to the ressentiment to the wretched.2 It is ill-advised to rigidly oppose reason to ressentiment. Indeed, to paraphrase Pascal, ressentiment has its reasons that reason doesn’t know. Becoming acquainted with ressentiment’s reasons, the justifications for its proclivities, is an arduous task. The dialectic imbrication of self and ressentiment leaves neither unaltered by their continuing co-constitution. Ressentiment is neither fully distinct from the self, nor does it exhaust that self; other feelings and non-affective qualities continue to contribute to my being. In its rawness ressentiment can be overwhelming, and thus risk confirming all the fears of its detractors. But ressentiment can also be fashioned or dialecticized. Its brute energies are at once annulled and retained.

Living with ressentiment underscores the dynamic gap between myself and my feeling of indignation. The non-identity between self and ressentiment, even as they are co- constituted, allows us to style and harness ressentiment’s affective powers.

Having said that, we should not forget that the dynamism between the two is not unidirectional. We might say that ressentiment is consubstantial with the self. Our self fashions ressentiment, giving it form, either private or public, and fashions ourself/our cause through ressentiment, but ressentiment also fashions our self and our cause.

If the self can intervene and re-channel ressentiment for more progressive ends, ressentiment can empower you to push back against a too reasonable, measured, or compromised self, caught up in the tyranny of consensus and agreement.
And to recall,

the greatest ruse of colonizers and liberals alike is to convince the wretched to hate themselves—tormented by imagos that unconsciously gnaw at their being—and unwittingly agree to their own disenfranchisement by binding them to the predominant ideology.

A ressentiment- induced No! is tantamount to an affective rebellion, a counter-force, short-circuiting the (neo)colonizer’s racist libidinal economy. It signals the disobedient reason of the wretched and jolts the self out of her moderate slumber.

The ressentimental I is a freedom fighter; she makes no pretense of innocence and loathes virtue-signaling. She resists and strikes at her opponents, culturally and martially, announcing to them, as Fanon does, that “the last shall be irst.”3 In this sense, ressentiment—of the recalcitrant wretched and those who commit themselves to their cause—inculcates a generative intolerance of masters and settlers (it cancels and preserves the stinging negativity of Nietzschean ressentiment)—of those who thrive on the backs of the most vulnerable, and of those who defeatistly or complacently accept conformism and complicity with such unjust systems, who modestly enjoy the economic and libidinal benefits of not being wretched (and of hating the wretched). Living with ressentiment, especially in its public use, also means learning to live with the other’s ressentiment—the ressentiment of fellow wretched and potentially the ressentiment-to-come of those in positions of power and privilege, enticing them to self-sacrifice, defect, and join the cause, the struggle for justice and freedom, since, as Houria Bouteldja avers, “if your history made you white, nothing is forcing you to stay that way.”4 Wilderson’s junior partners are no exception. Your race—who/ what you have been rendered—is not destiny.

Care for the unsanctioned other entails a reckoning with your sanctioned self. Ressentiment reminds you that you are not tethered to your organic community and given self, limited, in your everyday practices, to the private use of reason; you are not an “automaton,”

as Frédéric Gros would put it.5 It incites us to action, to forge new desires; it all starts “with an internal divestment,”6 with a political deviation from the symbolic order’s pleasure principle. The volatility of ressentiment—its imposing ungovernability—also helps to explain the challenges facing solidarity movements. The lure of wounded attachment feels at times too irresistible—it authorizes anger, and provides you with identitarian and institutional support when you need it most. But
another ressentiment exists
as well,
one that refuses the vicissitudes of recognition and avoids the conversion of ressentiment into victimhood
which
, I’ll say it again,
is only ever an iteration of the human(ist) grammar of suffering.

It is a ressentiment that both delights in its unruliness and out-of-jointness, and makes the conditions of unacceptability and nonconformity a universal problem— not just my own. Yet even when we move away from an identity-based solidarity (your suffering is my suffering), the problem remains that in your general orientation to the world, you participate, unknowingly, in my erasure, locking me in the position of the unthought. The cause of my ressentiment remains unintelligible to you. This is the challenge that Critical Black Studies have justly brought to the forefront of our thinking.
The liberation of humanity
, if there is such a thing,

must involve the radical destruction of the human and its reinvention. A reckoning with the other’s ressentiment—attentiveness to her form of ensnarement in this world—is indispensable for solidarity’s future. Though the wretched share a certain proximity to, and experience of, the hellish zone of nonbeing, how they find themselves in but not of this world, deprived of dignity and protection, is modulated differently, by varying historical-geographical contexts and interlocking structures of inequality. And if ressentiment’s contours do change in the interaction with the self, its shape will surely mutate in unexpected fashion once the affect of the wretched is elevated to the level of the ressentimental “we.” A solidarity movement worthy of its name must take the irreducibility and fraught malleability of ressentiment as axiomatic without simultaneously transforming it into an insurmountable ontological obstacle— whence the wayward exercise of putting it to public use.
